back: Split the word into prefix, root, and suffix. Use the meaning of each recognizable piece to build a reasonable definition, then use that reasoning to eliminate two or three clearly wrong options before choosing among what remains.

front: Prefix: bene-
back: Means good or well. Appears in benevolent, meaning wishing others well, and beneficial, meaning producing a good result. The everyday word benefit shares the same piece and helps you recall the meaning quickly.

front: Prefix: mal-
back: Means bad or wrong. Appears in malicious, meaning intending harm, and malfunction, meaning working badly. A word starting with mal- almost always signals something negative, defective, or wrongful.

front: Prefix: anti-
back: Means against. Appears in antagonist, one who works against another, and antidote, something that counters a poison. Look for anti- whenever a word describes opposition, resistance, or working against something.

front: Prefix: pre-
back: Means before. Appears in premeditated, meaning thought out beforehand, and precede, meaning to come before. Common in report writing whenever you describe planning or events that happened prior to something else.

front: Prefix: post-
back: Means after. Appears in postmortem, meaning after death, and posterior, meaning situated behind. It is the direct opposite of pre-, useful for placing events in sequence within a report.

front: Prefix: con- or co-
back: Means with or together. Appears in cooperate, meaning to work together, and concur, meaning to agree together. Useful for spotting words describing collaboration, agreement, or shared action between people.

front: Prefix: de-
back: Often means down, away, or reversal. Appears in detain, meaning to hold back, and devalue, meaning to lower the value of. Context decides whether it signals removal, reduction, or reversal of an action.

front: Prefix: in- or un-
back: Usually means not, as in incoherent, not making sense, or unlawful, not lawful. Watch for in- also meaning into, as in inject, so confirm the rest of the word before assuming a negative meaning.

front: Root: cred
back: Relates to belief or trust. Appears in credible, meaning believable, and credentials, meaning things that earn trust. Any word built on cred concerns whether a person or statement can be trusted.

front: Root: dict
back: Relates to speaking or saying. Appears in dictate, meaning to say aloud for recording, and predict, meaning to say beforehand. Look for dict in words about speech, statements, or declarations.

front: Root: duc or duct
back: Relates to leading. Appears in conduct, meaning to lead or direct, and induce, meaning to lead into a state or action. Useful for words describing guidance or causing something to happen.

front: Root: spect or spec
back: Relates to seeing or looking. Appears in inspect, meaning to look into closely, and spectator, meaning one who looks on. Common in report writing for words about observation and examination.

front: Root: vid or vis
back: Also relates to seeing. Appears in evident, meaning clearly seen, and visible, meaning able to be seen. A second seeing-root alongside spect, useful whenever spect does not fit the word.

front: Root: ject
back: Relates to throwing. Appears in eject, meaning to throw out, and projectile, meaning something thrown forward. Look for ject when a word involves forceful expulsion or propulsion of something.

front: Root: mit or mis
back: Relates to sending. Appears in transmit, meaning to send across, and dismiss, meaning to send away. Useful for words about communication being passed along or someone being sent off.

front: Suffix: -ology
back: Means the study of. Appears in criminology, the study of crime, and psychology, the study of the mind. Signals that a word names an academic or systematic field of knowledge.

front: Suffix: -ist
back: Means one who practices or does something. Appears in words naming a specialist or a person performing a field of work. Turns a field or action into the person who carries it out.

front: Suffix: -ify or -fy
back: Means to make or cause. Appears in verify, meaning to make true, that is, to confirm, and clarify, meaning to make clear. Signals a verb describing bringing about a particular state.

front: Suffix: -tion or -sion
back: Turns a verb into a noun describing an action or its result. Appears in detention, the act of detaining, and apprehension, the act of apprehending, or a feeling of dread. A common ending in report-writing nouns.

front: Credible versus credulous: how do they differ?
back: Credible means believable and worthy of trust, as in a credible witness. Credulous means overly willing to believe things, that is, gullible, as in a credulous person who falls for scams. Same root, opposite direction of trust.

front: Affect versus effect: how do they differ as vocabulary?
back: As a noun, affect refers to an observable emotional expression, as in a flat affect. Effect as a noun refers to a result or outcome, as in the effect of the medication. They name genuinely different concepts, not just a spelling quirk.

front: Elicit versus illicit: how do they differ?
back: Elicit means to draw out or bring forth a response, as in eliciting a statement from a witness. Illicit means illegal or forbidden. They sound almost identical, which is exactly why the exam plants one as a trap for the other.

front: Complement versus compliment: how do they differ?
back: Complement means to complete or go well with something, as in evidence that complements a witness statement. Compliment means praise or a flattering remark. Different meanings hiding behind nearly identical spelling.

front: Discreet versus discrete: how do they differ?
back: Discreet means careful and unobtrusive, showing good judgment about what to reveal. Discrete means separate and distinct from other things. They sound identical when spoken, so meaning must be judged from context, not sound.

front: Flaunt versus flout: how do they differ?
back: Flaunt means to show off, to display something proudly. Flout means to openly disregard a rule, as in flouting a court order. One concerns display, the other concerns defiance, despite the similar look and sound.

front: What is the difference between denotation and connotation?
back: Denotation is a word's literal, dictionary definition. Connotation is the emotional shading, attitude, or judgment a word carries beyond that literal meaning. Two words can share a denotation while carrying very different connotations.

front: Frugal versus stingy: what does this pair teach about connotation?
back: Both describe someone careful with money, so they share a denotation. Frugal carries a positive or neutral connotation, describing someone sensible and disciplined. Stingy carries a negative connotation, describing someone unpleasantly tight-fisted. Tone is what separates the two.

front: Assertive versus aggressive versus arrogant: how do connotations separate them?
back: Assertive means expressing yourself confidently and directly without being pushed around, a positive tone. Aggressive adds a harsher, hostile edge implying a willingness to attack. Arrogant implies an unearned sense of superiority. Same general territory, very different emotional weight.

front: What two-step process finds the best synonym on a hard question?
back: First use denotation to eliminate any option that is flatly wrong in literal meaning. Second use connotation to choose between the remaining close options by matching emotional tone. Denotation narrows the field, connotation picks the winner.

front: What should you do before locking in an option that looks instantly familiar?
back: Pause for one extra second and state that option's actual definition in your head. If you only recognized it because it looks or sounds like the target word, treat that instant match as a warning sign, not a shortcut.

front: What should you do when none of the four options feels like a perfect synonym?
back: Remember the question asks for the closest meaning, not an identical one. Go through each option and name the specific flaw, too strong, too weak, wrong connotation, or a different concept, rather than relying on a vague feeling that it is not quite right.

front: Reluctant versus refusing: what is the difference in degree?
back: Refusing describes an active, completed decision not to do something. Reluctant describes hesitation and unwillingness, someone who may still do the thing but is dragging their feet. The gap is in degree, not just in raw meaning.

front: Vocabulary word: commence
back: Means to begin or start formally. A more formal register alternative to start, commonly used in report writing, as in the officer commenced the investigation at 0800 hours.

front: Vocabulary word: ascertain
back: Means to find out or establish with certainty through checking or investigation. A formal alternative to figure out, as in officers ascertained the vehicle's registered owner before proceeding.

front: Vocabulary word: corroborate
back: Means to confirm or support a statement or claim using additional independent evidence. Used when a second source backs up a witness account, as in the security footage corroborated her statement.

front: Vocabulary word: belligerent
back: Means hostile and aggressive, ready to fight. A precise formal alternative to the vague word angry, signalling specifically that a subject was combative rather than merely upset or annoyed.

front: Vocabulary word: erratic
back: Means unpredictable and lacking a consistent pattern, wandering irregularly. Used to describe behaviour or movement that is inconsistent, as in the driver's erratic lane changes prompted a traffic stop.

front: Vocabulary word: evasive
back: Means avoiding direct answers or honest engagement, deliberately vague. Used to describe someone dodging questions, as in the subject gave evasive answers about his whereabouts that evening.

front: Vocabulary word: coherent
back: Means making logical sense, able to speak or think clearly and consistently. Its opposite, incoherent, describes speech or thought that does not make sense, a distinction often noted in impairment assessments.

front: What does the Navigation and Map Reading section actually measure?
back: It measures whether you can follow written rules exactly under time pressure, not real driving knowledge or traffic law. The map is a simplified grid with one-way arrows and closures; everything you need is printed on it.

front: True or false: you should use real-world driving instinct to fix an unclear route on the map.
back: False. The map is the entire universe of truth. If a street is not marked one-way, treat it as two-way. If it is not marked closed, treat it as open. Never add or ignore rules that are not shown.

front: What are the only two special markings you need to look for on an APCAT navigation map?
back: One-way arrows, which restrict a street segment to a single direction, and X marks or closure symbols, which block a street segment entirely in both directions.

front: What is the correct order of operations before comparing any route options?
back: First find every one-way arrow, second find every closure or X mark, third locate the Start and destination points, and only after that read the four route options.

front: Why does the exam reward finding arrows and closures before reading the options?
back: Candidates who jump straight to comparing routes often half convince themselves an option is shortest before noticing a one-way arrow that eliminates it. Front-loading rule-finding prevents that mistake.

front: How should you phrase a one-way rule to yourself while scanning a map?
back: Say it as a full sentence, such as "Elm Street between 2nd and 3rd only allows travel northbound." Naming the exact street, cross streets, and direction locks the rule into memory before you look at options.

front: Does a closure on Oak Street between 3rd and 4th affect Oak Street between 4th and 5th?
back: No. A closure applies only to the exact block segment named, between two specific intersections. Adjacent segments of the same street are unaffected unless separately marked.

front: What should your mental checklist look like after scanning a map, before reading options?
back: A short list naming each restriction exactly, for example "Spruce Street one-way eastbound between 1st and 2nd. Birch Street closed between 3rd and 4th. Nothing else restricted."

front: What phrase in almost every question stem is a trap if read too quickly?
back: "Shortest route." The exam always means shortest legal route, even when the word legal is not repeated, so pure distance can never be compared before legality is checked.

front: A route has the fewest total blocks but drives one block against a one-way arrow. Is it a valid answer?
back: No. An illegal shortcut is disqualified before distance is even compared, no matter how short it would have been on an unrestricted map.

front: Describe the typical pattern of four route options in this section.
back: Usually one is genuinely shortest but illegal, one is legal but longer than necessary, one may combine both problems, and one is fully legal and truly shortest. Your job is to eliminate rule breakers first.

front: What is Step One of the elimination method?
back: Trace each of the four options segment by segment against your checklist. At each segment ask only whether it breaks a one-way rule or crosses a closed block; if yes, eliminate that whole option immediately.

front: In Step One of elimination, once a single segment breaks a rule, what should you do?
back: Cross the entire option out immediately and move to the next one. You do not need to check its remaining segments or think about its length at all.

front: What is Step Two of the elimination method?
back: After checking all four options, see how many remain legal. If exactly one option survives, it is the answer by default and you do not need to compare lengths at all.

front: What is Step Three of the elimination method?
back: If more than one option survives the legality check, compare their lengths in block segments. The legal survivor with the fewest segments is the correct answer.

front: Why is checking legality before length faster than checking both at once?
back: It turns a hard four-way comparison into at most a two or three way length comparison among only the legal survivors, saving time and preventing the mistake of picking a shortest-looking but illegal route.

front: What does one segment mean when counting a route's length?
back: One move from an intersection to the very next adjacent intersection, in any of the four directions. An instruction like "go south three blocks" counts as three segments, not one.

front: Why should you not judge route length by eye on this section?
back: APCAT maps are not drawn to scale; block lengths on the page can vary for layout reasons even though they represent equal blocks in the scenario. Always count segments instead of trusting how long a line looks.

front: What is a good habit for tallying a route's length while tracing it?
back: Write a running total after each leg rather than adding everything at the end from memory. For "east two blocks, south one block, east one block, south two blocks," jot down 2, then 3, then 4, then 6.

front: What is a "jog" in a route description, and why is it a common trap?
back: A short detour off the direct path and back onto it again. It might only add two extra segments, which can look deceptively close to the shortest option if you eyeball the map instead of counting.

front: If two legal survivor routes tie at the same segment count, what should you do?
back: Treat the tie as a cue to recount both routes carefully, since test writers usually design the map so exactly one option reaches the true minimum. A clean tie is rare and worth double-checking.

front: Mini scenario: a one-way arrow points east on Maple between 1st and 2nd. A route goes west from 2nd and Maple to 1st and Maple. Legal or illegal?
back: Illegal. The route travels against the marked direction on that exact segment, so it is eliminated on that single move regardless of how the rest of the route looks.

front: Mini scenario: Larch Street is closed between 1st and 2nd. A route travels from 2nd and Larch straight through to 1st and Larch. Legal or illegal?
back: Illegal. Driving through a closed block segment eliminates the whole route completely, exactly the same as a one-way violation does, regardless of the route's total length.

front: Mini scenario: 2nd Street is one-way southbound between Oak and Fir. A route travels south from Oak and 2nd to Fir and 2nd. Legal or illegal?
back: Legal. The route travels in the same direction the arrow allows, so this segment passes the check. Continue tracing the rest of the route against the checklist before deciding on the whole option.

front: Mini scenario: a route avoids every marked one-way street and every closure, but loops three extra blocks south and back north. Is it the correct answer?
back: Not necessarily. It is fully legal, but if a shorter legal route also exists among the options, the shorter one wins. Legality alone does not guarantee the shortest answer.

front: Mini scenario: Option one is shortest but illegal, Option two is legal but longer, Option three is both illegal and longer. What must Option four be to be correct?
back: Option four must be both fully legal and truly the shortest among the legal options. Being merely legal, or merely short, is not enough on its own.

front: Mini scenario: Aspen Street is one-way westbound between 2nd and 3rd. A route goes east from 2nd and Aspen to 3rd and Aspen. Legal or illegal?
back: Illegal. This segment travels eastbound directly against the westbound arrow, so the entire option is eliminated on that one move, no matter how efficient the rest of the path looks.

front: Mini scenario: a route travels along Willow Street the whole way and never touches a restricted stretch of Aspen or a closed stretch of Birch. Legal or illegal?
back: Legal. A route that never crosses any marked restriction passes the legality check entirely, regardless of how many total segments it takes to reach the destination.

front: Mini scenario: two legal routes remain after elimination, one totalling six segments and one totalling eight segments. Which is correct?
back: The six-segment route is correct. Once legality has narrowed the field, the surviving route with the fewest block segments is always the answer.

front: Mini scenario: a legal route includes a needless jog north one block and back south one block off the direct path. What does this cost it?
back: Two extra segments compared to the most direct legal path. It stays legal, but the extra segments likely make it longer than another legal option, so it is probably a trap answer.

front: What is the very first thing you should do when a new navigation map appears?
back: Scan the entire map for one-way arrows before anything else. Note the exact street, cross streets, and direction for each one you find.

front: After finding all one-way arrows, what is the second thing you should scan for?
back: Every X mark or closure symbol on the map, noting the exact block segment each one blocks, meaning the two intersections it sits between.

front: True or false: a one-way violation and a closure disqualify a route equally.
back: True. Whether a segment breaks a one-way rule or crosses a closed block, the effect is identical: the entire route option is eliminated on that single segment.

front: What kind of outside knowledge, if any, do you need for this section?
back: None. You need no outside knowledge of traffic law, road signs, or real city layouts. Every rule you need is printed directly on the map and in the route descriptions.

front: Why is this section best described as a logic puzzle with a map skin?
back: Because success depends on carefully applying a small set of stated rules and counting accurately, not on real driving experience. It rewards checklist discipline over real-world intuition.

front: Complete the method: check legality first, then compare what?
back: Lengths, but only among the routes that already passed the legality check. Never compare the length of an illegal route to a legal one, since the illegal one is already disqualified.

front: A route instruction reads "south three blocks, east two blocks." How many total segments is that?
back: Five segments. Add the block counts within each instruction rather than counting the number of instructions or turns; three blocks south plus two blocks east equals five moves total.

front: Why might a candidate wrongly pick an illegal route as the answer?
back: Because they measured pure distance first and picked the option with the fewest blocks, without checking whether it obeyed every one-way arrow and closure. Checking legality first prevents this exact mistake.

front: What single question should you ask at each segment while tracing a route in Step One?
back: Does this move break a one-way rule, or does it cross a closed block? A yes to either question eliminates the entire option immediately.

front: Mini scenario: after elimination, exactly one route option remains fully legal. Do you still need to count its segments?
back: No. A lone legal survivor wins by default. Counting segments only matters when more than one option survives the legality check.

front: What three moves should you repeat for every navigation question on the real exam?
back: Find every one-way arrow and closure before reading options, eliminate any option breaking a rule on even one segment, then count block segments carefully on the remaining legal options and pick the lowest total.

front: What are the five steps for solving any APCAT word problem?
back: Identify what is being asked, identify the given numbers and what each means, write the expression or equation, solve the arithmetic step by step, then sanity check the answer against the original question.

front: In the five-step word problem method, what does step one require?
back: Find the question in the problem and state exactly what quantity you need to find, such as a time, a distance, a percentage, a count, or a cost.

front: In the five-step word problem method, what does step two require?
back: Pull out every given number in the problem and label what each one represents, since word problems often bury useful numbers inside irrelevant details.

front: In the five-step word problem method, what does step three require?
back: Write the expression or equation that connects the given numbers to the quantity you are solving for, applying the correct formula for that type of problem.

front: In the five-step word problem method, what does step four require?
back: Solve the equation one operation at a time, keeping careful track of your units throughout the calculation so nothing gets mismatched along the way.

front: In the five-step word problem method, what does step five require, and why do most candidates skip it?
back: Sanity check the answer against the original question by asking whether the number makes sense in the real world. Most candidates skip this step, but it catches wrong signs, misplaced decimals, and swapped numbers.

front: What formula connects distance, rate, and time?
back: Distance equals rate multiplied by time, written D equals R times T. Knowing any two of the three values lets you solve directly for the third one.

front: How do you find time when you know distance and rate?
back: Divide distance by rate. For example, a trip of 84 kilometres at 56 kilometres per hour takes 84 divided by 56, which equals 1.5 hours, or 1 hour 30 minutes.

front: How do you find rate, or speed, when you know distance and time?
back: Divide distance by time. This isolates the rate from the distance-rate-time relationship and gives the average speed needed to cover that distance in that amount of time.

front: In a meeting problem, where two vehicles start apart and travel toward each other, how do you find their combined closing speed?
back: Add the two speeds together. The gap between the vehicles closes at a rate equal to the sum of their speeds, so time to meet equals the starting distance divided by that sum.

front: In a catch-up problem, where one vehicle chases another travelling the same direction, how do you find the closing speed?
back: Subtract the slower speed from the faster speed. Unlike a meeting problem the speeds do not add, because both vehicles move the same way and only the difference closes the gap.

front: What is the formula for percentage change?
back: The new value minus the old value, divided by the old value, then multiplied by 100. This gives the percentage the value rose or fell relative to where it started.

front: What is the formula for finding what percentage one number is of another?
back: Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100. This tells you what share the smaller number represents of the larger total it belongs to.

front: When calculating a percentage decrease, should you divide the difference by the original value or the new value?
back: Always divide by the original, older value, never the new one. A drop from 350 to 280 is a decrease of 70, measured against 350, giving 20 percent, not against 280.

front: What is the method for splitting a total according to a given ratio?
back: Add the parts of the ratio to find the total number of shares, divide the total amount by that number of shares to get the value of one share, then multiply that value by each ratio part.

front: What is the method for scaling a known ratio to a new total?
back: Divide the new total by the matching known quantity to find a scaling factor, then multiply every other part of the original ratio by that same factor to keep the relationship unchanged.

front: What is the recommended method for turning an algebra word problem into an equation?
back: Assign a letter to the unknown you know least about, write an equation that captures the sentence exactly, then gather the unknown terms on one side and the plain numbers on the other before dividing to isolate the unknown.

front: Why does 'three more than double a number' translate to 2p plus 3 rather than 2 times (p plus 3)?
back: Doubling applies to the number alone before the 3 is added on, so the operations must stay in that order. Writing 2 times (p plus 3) would double the 3 as well, changing the meaning of the sentence.

front: What are the three most common conversion factors for APCAT unit conversion problems?
back: 60 minutes in an hour, 1,000 metres in a kilometre, and 3.6 to convert a speed in metres per second directly into kilometres per hour.

front: What is the fast mental math shortcut for finding 15 percent of a number?
back: Find 10 percent by moving the decimal point one place left, then add half of that 10 percent value, since 5 percent is half of 10 percent. The two amounts together equal 15 percent.

front: What is the fast mental math shortcut for finding 20 percent of a number?
back: Find 10 percent first, by moving the decimal point one place left, then double that value. Doubling the 10 percent figure gives you 20 percent directly.

front: What is the fast mental math shortcut for finding 5 percent of a number?
back: Find 10 percent first, by moving the decimal point one place left, then take half of that value. Halving the 10 percent figure gives you 5 percent directly.

front: What is the fast mental math shortcut for finding 25 percent of a number?
back: Take one quarter of the total directly, by dividing the number by 4. This avoids building up from 10 percent and is usually the fastest route to a 25 percent figure.

front: What is the round and adjust technique for fast mental multiplication?
back: Split a harder multiplication into friendly pieces, usually a times-10 part and a times-5 or times-1 part, then add the pieces together. This is almost always faster than multiplying the full numbers directly.

front: Why should you estimate the size of an answer before calculating it precisely?
back: A rough estimate is your fastest sanity check. It catches decimal errors and misplaced operations immediately, before they cost a mark, by giving a sense of roughly how large the real answer should be.

front: What should you do if one word problem is taking far longer than the others in the timed section?
back: Mark your best guess, flag it if the format allows, and move on. Protect your average pace across the whole section rather than spending too long defending your record on one hard question.

front: 156 case files need to be split evenly among 4 analysts. How many files does each analyst review?
back: 39 files each. Divide 156 by 4 to get 39. Check: 39 times 4 equals 156, matching the total, and 39 files is a reasonable individual workload.

front: A patrol car travels 84 kilometres at an average speed of 56 kilometres per hour. How long does the trip take?
back: 1 hour 30 minutes. Divide 84 by 56 to get 1.5 hours, then convert the 0.5 hour to minutes by multiplying by 60, giving 30 minutes. Check: 56 times 1.5 equals 84.

front: Two patrol units start 240 kilometres apart and drive toward each other at 55 km/h and 65 km/h. How long until they meet?
back: 2 hours. Add the speeds, 55 plus 65 equals 120 km/h combined, then divide the starting distance by that combined speed, 240 divided by 120 equals 2 hours. Check: 110 plus 130 equals 240.

front: A patrol car at 80 km/h chases a vehicle 40 kilometres ahead travelling the same direction at 60 km/h. How long to catch it?
back: 2 hours. Since both travel the same direction, subtract the speeds, 80 minus 60 equals 20 km/h closing speed, then divide the gap by that difference, 40 divided by 20 equals 2 hours.

front: Reported incidents rose from 220 in March to 253 in April. What was the percentage increase?
back: 15 percent. Subtract 220 from 253 to get 33, then divide 33 by the original value 220 and multiply by 100. Check: 15 percent of 220 is 33, and 220 plus 33 equals 253.

front: Of 220 March incidents, 55 happened on a weekend. What percentage of March's incidents were on a weekend?
back: 25 percent. Divide the part, 55, by the whole, 220, then multiply by 100. Check: 25 percent of 220 is 55, matching the given number, and one quarter of a month is plausible.

front: A value drops from 350 to 280. What is the percentage decrease, and against which value is it measured?
back: 20 percent, measured against the original value of 350. The decrease of 70 is divided by 350, not by the new value 280, giving 70 divided by 350 times 100, which equals 20 percent.

front: 84 recruits are split into two groups in a ratio of 3 to 4. How many go into each group?
back: 36 and 48. Add the ratio parts, 3 plus 4 equals 7 shares, then divide 84 by 7 to get 12 per share. Group one gets 3 times 12, which is 36; group two gets 48.

front: 96 supplies are split between two units in a ratio of 5 to 3. How many does each unit receive?
back: 60 and 36. Add the ratio parts, 5 plus 3 equals 8 shares, then divide 96 by 8 to get 12 per share. One unit gets 5 times 12, which is 60; the other gets 36.

front: Staffing guidelines call for 2 supervisors for every 9 officers. A shift has 45 officers. How many supervisors are needed?
back: 10 supervisors. Divide the new officer count by the standard one, 45 divided by 9 equals a scaling factor of 5, then multiply the standard 2 supervisors by 5 to get 10.

front: A workshop needs 3 mechanics for every 8 vehicles serviced. If the fleet grows to 56 vehicles, how many mechanics are needed?
back: 21 mechanics. Divide the new vehicle count by the standard one, 56 divided by 8 equals a scaling factor of 7, then multiply the standard 3 mechanics by 7 to get 21.

front: Chen issued 3 more tickets than double Patel's total, and together they issued 39 tickets. How many did each officer issue?
back: Patel issued 12, Chen issued 27. Let p equal Patel's tickets, so p plus (2p plus 3) equals 39, giving 3p equals 36, so p equals 12. Chen issued 2 times 12 plus 3, which is 27.

front: A witness estimates a vehicle's speed at 20 metres per second. What is that speed in kilometres per hour?
back: 72 kilometres per hour. Multiply the metres-per-second value by the conversion factor 3.6, since 20 times 3.6 equals 72. This is below a 100 km/h posted limit, so the figure is realistic.

front: A call's response time is recorded as 105 minutes. Express that as hours and minutes, and as a decimal number of hours.
back: 1 hour 45 minutes, or 1.75 hours as a decimal. 60 minutes make one hour, leaving 45 minutes over, and 105 divided by 60 equals 1.75, since 45 minutes is three quarters of an hour.

front: Using the 10-percent-then-half shortcut, what is 15 percent of 340?
back: 51. Find 10 percent of 340, which is 34, then add half of that, which is 17. 34 plus 17 equals 51, matching the direct calculation of 340 times 0.15.

front: What three checks should you run on a number sequence, and in what order?
back: Check differences between consecutive terms first, then ratios between consecutive terms, and only if neither is consistent, check whether the sequence is two interleaved patterns running side by side.

front: Why is it risky to lock in an arithmetic rule after checking only the first gap in a sequence?
back: A single matching gap can happen by coincidence in a sequence that is actually two interleaved patterns. Checking only the first gap is a common way candidates get fooled into a wrong rule.

front: What is a difference pattern, and how do you find one?
back: An arithmetic pattern where the same number is added or subtracted at every step. Subtract each term from the one after it; if every result matches across the whole sequence, you have found it.

front: What is a ratio pattern, and how do you find one?
back: A geometric pattern where each term is multiplied by the same factor. Divide each term by the term before it; if every quotient matches across the whole sequence, you have found it.

front: 5, 11, 17, 23, 29 - what is the rule and the next term?
back: Add 6 each step. 11-5=6, 17-11=6, 23-17=6, 29-23=6, all consistent. The next term is 29+6=35.

front: 2, 6, 18, 54, 162 - what is the rule and the next term?
back: Multiply by 3 each step. 6/2=3, 18/6=3, 54/18=3, 162/54=3, all consistent. The next term is 162x3=486.

front: 100, 90, 80, 70 - what is the rule and the next term?
back: Subtract 10 each step. 90-100=-10, 80-90=-10, 70-80=-10, all consistent. The next term is 70-10=60.

front: 7, 14, 28, 56 - what is the rule and the next term?
back: Multiply by 2 each step. 14/7=2, 28/14=2, 56/28=2, all consistent. The next term is 56x2=112.

front: What does it mean for a sequence to be two interleaved patterns?
back: Two separate rules run at once inside one sequence, one through the odd-numbered positions and one through the even-numbered positions. Split the sequence into those two threads and check each one for its own difference or ratio rule.

front: 9, 20, 11, 16, 13, 12 - split into two threads and find the seventh term.
back: Odd positions 9, 11, 13 rise by 2 each step. Even positions 20, 16, 12 fall by 4 each step. The seventh term continues the odd thread: 13+2=15.

front: When should you suspect a sequence is actually two interleaved threads rather than one rule?
back: When the differences and the ratios between consecutive terms are not consistent across the whole sequence, especially if the sequence looked arithmetic for the first couple of gaps and then stopped matching.

front: B, L, D, J, F, H, H, F - split into two threads and find the ninth term.
back: Convert to positions 2, 12, 4, 10, 6, 8, 8, 6. Odd positions 2, 4, 6, 8 rise by 2 each step. Even positions 12, 10, 8, 6 fall by 2 each step. The ninth term continues the odd thread: 8+2=10, which is J.

front: What single fix makes letter sequences as easy to check as number sequences?
back: Convert every letter to its position in the alphabet, A=1 through Z=26. The letter sequence becomes a number sequence, and you check it with the exact same difference, ratio, and interleaved-thread order.

front: What position is the letter M in the alphabet?
back: M is the 13th letter of the alphabet. Counting from A=1, B=2, C=3 and onward in order gets you to M=13.

front: What position is the letter R in the alphabet?
back: R is the 18th letter of the alphabet. Counting from A=1 in order, or from around the halfway point, gets you to R=18.

front: What is the shortcut for finding the alphabet position of a letter in the back half of the alphabet?
back: Subtract the letter's position counted from the end of the alphabet from 27. For example, W is the fourth-last letter, so 27 minus 4 equals 23, which is W's position.

front: Using the back-half shortcut, what position is the letter Y?
back: Y is the second-last letter of the alphabet, so 27 minus 2 equals 25. Y's alphabet position is 25.

front: After converting a letter sequence to numbers, what checking order do you use?
back: The exact same order used for any number sequence: differences first, then ratios, then a check for two interleaved threads if neither of the first two checks produces a consistent rule.

front: C, F, I, L - what is the rule and the next letter?
back: Convert to positions 3, 6, 9, 12. Each rises by 3, skipping two letters every step. The next position is 12+3=15, which converts back to the letter O.

front: Z, X, V, T - what is the rule and the next letter?
back: Convert to positions 26, 24, 22, 20. Each falls by 2, skipping one letter every step. The next position is 20-2=18, which converts back to the letter R.

front: B, D, F, I, J - one letter breaks the skip-by-2 pattern. Which one, and what should it be?
back: Convert to positions 2, 4, 6, 9, 10. The established rule adds 2 each step, so the fourth term should be 8, letter H, not 9, letter I. The fifth term, 10 or J, still fits the rule from the corrected value, confirming I is the outlier.

front: What must you always do when a sequence pairs a letter with a digit, such as A1, C3, E5?
back: Check the letters and the numbers as two separate lines. Convert the letters to alphabet positions and check their own pattern, then check the attached numbers' pattern on its own, since the two parts do not always follow the same rule.

front: B2, D4, F6, H8 - what is the next term?
back: Letters B, D, F, H convert to 2, 4, 6, 8, rising by 2 each step, so the next letter is 10, which is J. The numbers 2, 4, 6, 8 also rise by 2 each step, so the next number is 10. The next term is J10.

front: Why is a trap sequence pairing letters that skip by 1 position with numbers that double each time so dangerous?
back: The two parts follow completely different rule types. A candidate who only checks the easier-to-see numeric pattern can get a confident wrong answer without ever verifying that the letters follow the same, or a different, logic.

front: What is the single biggest mistake candidates make on odd-one-out questions?
back: Trying to spot the outlier by eye. A pattern broken by a small amount, such as one number off by just 1, is easy to miss visually under time pressure with a countdown clock running.

front: What is the reliable method for finding the odd one out in a set?
back: Establish the rule from terms you can verify, then test every remaining item against that rule individually, one at a time, rather than scanning the set and waiting for something to jump out.

front: 4, 8, 16, 33, 64 - which term breaks the pattern, and what should it be?
back: The first two ratios, 8/4 and 16/8, both equal 2, establishing a multiply-by-2 rule. Applied forward, 16x2=32, not 33, so 33 is the broken term. Checking the final term, 32x2=64 matches the actual 64, confirming the rule and that 33 should have been 32.

front: Why does testing the term after a suspected broken term matter in an odd-one-out check?
back: If the rule still holds for the term past the error, that proves the pattern is real and survives the mistake, rather than being a coincidence that happened to stop working right where you got suspicious.

front: In an odd-one-out set made of several short sequences rather than one long sequence, how do you find the one that does not fit?
back: Find the rule that the majority of the short sequences share, then test each remaining sequence against that rule individually. Never rely on which sequence looks different at a glance.

front: What is step one of the six-step pattern method when a sequence contains letters?
back: Convert every letter to its alphabet position before doing anything else, writing the numbers directly above or below the letters so you are not holding the conversion in your head while checking for a pattern.

front: What is step two of the six-step pattern method?
back: Write out the difference between every pair of consecutive terms across the whole sequence, not just the first pair, lined up underneath the terms so you can see all of them at once.

front: What are steps three and four of the six-step pattern method?
back: Step three: if every difference is the same, you have an arithmetic pattern and are done. Step four: if not, write out the ratio between every consecutive pair; if every ratio matches, you have a geometric pattern.

front: What is step five of the six-step pattern method?
back: If neither the differences nor the ratios are consistent across the whole sequence, split it into two threads, the odd-numbered positions and the even-numbered positions, and run the difference and ratio checks on each thread separately.

front: What is step six, the final step, of the six-step pattern method?
back: Apply the rule you found to every term in the sequence, including terms you have not directly used yet, before locking in your answer. This catches a rule that fit by coincidence but breaks down later in the sequence.

front: What is the first common trap in pattern recognition questions?
back: A sequence that looks arithmetic for the first two or three terms because the early differences happen to match by coincidence, when the sequence is actually two interleaved patterns running side by side.

front: 3, 9, 15, 6, 27, 3 - the first two gaps both equal 6. What is the real rule, and what is the seventh term?
back: The pattern of 6, 6 suggests adding 6, predicting 21 next, but the actual term is 6. Split into threads: odd positions 3, 15, 27 add 12 each step; even positions 9, 6, 3 subtract 3 each step. The seventh term continues the odd thread: 27+12=39.

front: What is the second common trap in pattern recognition questions?
back: A sequence combining a letter pattern and a number pattern moving together, where a candidate correctly solves the easier part, usually the numbers, and forgets to verify that the other part follows the same or a different rule.

front: Both common traps in this section share the same root cause. What is it?
back: Stopping the checking process one step too early because an answer already feels confident. The fix for both is identical: write out every gap across the whole sequence and confirm the rule against every term before committing.

front: Why does the APCAT test pattern recognition with methodical checking rather than gut instinct?
back: Police services want recruits who can work through evidence and dispatch information methodically under pressure rather than jumping to the first conclusion that feels correct, which is the real skill this section measures.

front: About how long should a well-drilled pattern recognition item take once you know the checking order?
back: Under about fifteen seconds each, since almost every sequence on the test is built from a small handful of rule types you can check in a fixed, repeatable order.

front: True or false: two matching differences in a row is enough evidence to commit to an arithmetic rule.
back: False. Two matching differences can occur by coincidence in a sequence that is really two interleaved patterns, so you must check every gap across the whole sequence before committing to a rule.

front: A2, C4, E8, G16 - the letters and numbers follow different rule types. What is the next term?
back: Letters A, C, E, G convert to 1, 3, 5, 7, rising by 2 alphabet positions each step. Numbers 2, 4, 8, 16 double each step. The next letter is position 9, which is I, and the next number is 32, giving I32.

front: What does the Logical Reasoning and Deduction section actually test on the APCAT?
back: It tests whether a conclusion is strictly guaranteed by the given premises, not whether it sounds plausible or matches what usually happens on patrol. If the premises do not force the conclusion, the conclusion is wrong even if it seems reasonable.

front: In logic questions, what are a premise and a conclusion?
back: A premise is a statement given to you and treated as true for the question. The conclusion is the claim being tested. Your job is to check whether the premises force the conclusion to be true, rule it out, or leave it undecided.

front: What is the basic shape of a conditional statement, and what does it guarantee?
back: A conditional has the form 'if A, then B.' It guarantees that whenever A is true, B must also be true. It says nothing about what happens when A is false and does not claim A is the only way B can occur.

front: If a rule states 'if A, then B,' can B happen for a reason other than A?
back: Yes, unless the rule says 'if and only if.' 'If A, then B' guarantees B whenever A occurs, but it never claims A is the sole cause of B, so another factor could also produce B independently.

front: Given 'if A, then B,' what is the one valid way to flip the statement and keep it guaranteed true?
back: The contrapositive: 'if not B, then not A.' If B never occurred, then whatever guarantees B could not have occurred either, so A must be false. This is logically identical to the original rule.

front: Why is the contrapositive of 'if A, then B' always valid?
back: Because the original rule promises B whenever A is true. If B is false, A cannot be true, since a true A would have forced B to be true, contradicting the fact that B did not happen.

front: In conditional logic, what exactly is the fallacy called denying the antecedent?
back: Wrongly turning 'if A, then B' into 'if not A, then not B.' It is invalid because the rule never claimed A was the only path to B, so something else could still produce B even when A is false.

front: Rule: if a suspect flees on foot, a perimeter is set up. A suspect did not flee on foot. Is 'no perimeter was set up' a valid conclusion?
back: No, this is invalid. It denies the antecedent. The rule never said fleeing on foot was the only reason to set up a perimeter; another factor, like an armed threat, could still trigger one.

front: In conditional logic, what exactly is the fallacy called affirming the consequent?
back: Wrongly turning 'if A, then B' into 'if B, then A.' It is invalid because B being true does not reveal why it is true; something other than A could also have caused B.

front: Rule: if a vehicle is stolen, it is flagged in the database. A vehicle is flagged in the database. Is 'the vehicle was stolen' a valid conclusion?
back: No, this is invalid. It affirms the consequent. The rule only guarantees stolen vehicles get flagged; other reasons, such as a lien or a recall notice, could also cause a flag.

front: What is modus ponens, and is it a valid or invalid way to use a conditional?
back: Modus ponens applies a rule forward: given 'if A, then B' and A is true, you validly conclude B is true. It is always valid, since the rule directly guarantees B whenever A occurs.

front: Rule: if evidence is collected at a scene, it must be logged within 24 hours. Constable Okafor collected a knife as evidence. What follows?
back: The knife must be logged within 24 hours. This is valid modus ponens: A, evidence collected, is true, and the rule guarantees B, logged within 24 hours, whenever A is true.

front: Rule: if a call is classified active-threat, the on-call patrol supervisor personally oversees dispatch. Supervisor Alvarez, the on-call patrol supervisor that shift, did not personally oversee this dispatch. What must be true?
back: The call was not classified as active-threat. This is the valid contrapositive: no personal oversight guarantees the call was not active-threat, since active-threat calls always get personal oversight.

front: In a conditional logic question, why might an option be wrong even without committing a named fallacy?
back: The option can introduce information that appears nowhere in the premises, such as a specific new cause or actor. This is unsupported speculation, not a logical flip, and it is never guaranteed by the given rule alone.

front: When does a conditional rule guarantee both directions at once?
back: Only when the passage explicitly says 'if and only if.' A plain 'if A, then B' guarantees just one direction; treating it as reversible without that exact wording is always a mistake.

front: On the APCAT, what exactly is a categorical syllogism in this section?
back: Two statements about whole groups, usually using 'all,' 'some,' or 'no,' that let you reason about a specific member of one group. You must determine what is forced to be true for that member.

front: How does the two-circle test check whether a syllogism conclusion is valid?
back: Draw one circle for each group and place the item according to the premises. If the conclusion holds no matter how you draw the circles, it is valid. If you can draw them so the premises stay true but the conclusion is false, it is invalid.

front: All sworn officers must complete yearly requalification. Constable Diallo is a sworn officer. What must be true, and why is it valid?
back: Diallo must complete yearly requalification. The sworn officers circle sits entirely inside the requalification circle, so anyone placed in the sworn officers circle is automatically inside the requalification circle too.

front: In a categorical syllogism, what exactly is the undistributed middle fallacy?
back: Concluding that a member of the larger shared group must belong to the smaller group, when the premises never established that the shared trait belongs exclusively to that smaller group.

front: All detectives carry a badge. Officer Wren carries a badge. Is 'Officer Wren is a detective' a valid conclusion?
back: No, this is invalid, the undistributed middle. Wren only has to sit somewhere inside the badge-carrying circle. Patrol constables and sergeants also carry badges, so badge-carrying alone does not force detective status.

front: What syllogism shape is one of the most heavily tested traps on this section?
back: 'All X are Y, this item is Y, therefore this item is X.' It looks convincing but is invalid unless the passage also states that only X items are Y. Always draw the circles before trusting it.

front: Why is 'everyone who completes requalification is a sworn officer' not a guaranteed conclusion from 'all sworn officers must complete requalification'?
back: This reverses the premise without support. The rule only places sworn officers inside the requalification circle; it never claims the requalification circle contains nothing else, so civilians or other roles could also complete it.

front: Why is 'Constable Diallo has already completed this year's requalification' not a valid conclusion from a rule stating officers must complete it yearly?
back: The premise establishes an ongoing requirement, not a completed status. Nothing tells you whether Diallo has finished, is partway through, or has not started, so the statement could be false even with true premises.

front: What is the fastest, most reliable method for a 'which conclusion follows' question with four options?
back: Actively try to break each option by asking if it could be false while every premise stays true. Reject any option you can break. Whatever option survives every premise is the correct answer.

front: Every use-of-force report must be reviewed before the officer's shift ends. Constable Park filed one at 1400, shift ended 1800. Which conclusion must be true?
back: A sergeant reviewed Park's report before 1800 hours. This survives because the premise requires review before shift end for every report, and Park's shift ended at 1800, leaving no way around it.

front: In the Constable Park review scenario, why is 'the reviewing sergeant was on duty the entire shift' rejected as the answer?
back: Nothing in the premises describes the reviewing sergeant's schedule. A relief sergeant covering only part of the shift could have done the review, so the option could be false even with true premises.

front: What is a 'must be true' question asking you to find?
back: The one option that the premises absolutely guarantee, with no way for it to be false while the premises stay true. Nothing weaker, such as a merely possible option, qualifies as the answer.

front: What is a 'could be true' question asking you to find?
back: An option that the premises allow, meaning nothing in the passage rules it out, even though nothing forces it to be true either. It only needs to be consistent with the given premises.

front: What is a 'cannot be true' question asking you to find?
back: The one option that directly contradicts the premises, making it impossible given what you were told. It is the opposite target of a 'must be true' question.

front: Every night-shift patrol vehicle carries a first-aid kit and a spike strip. Unit 12 is on night shift this week. What must be true about Unit 12?
back: Unit 12 carries a first-aid kit. This is directly guaranteed, since every night-shift vehicle carries one and Unit 12 is confirmed to be a night-shift vehicle this week.

front: Using the Unit 12 night-shift premises, why does 'Unit 12 also carries a breathalyzer device' fit a could be true question?
back: The premises never mention breathalyzer devices at all, so nothing confirms or rules out the claim. It is possible but not guaranteed, which is exactly what a could be true answer requires.

front: Using the Unit 12 night-shift premises, why is 'Unit 12 carries no spike strip' the correct pick for a cannot be true question?
back: It directly contradicts the premise that every night-shift vehicle carries a spike strip. Since Unit 12 is a night-shift vehicle, this statement is impossible given the premises.

front: Why does misreading which of the three question types you are answering cost candidates points?
back: Each question type has a different correct answer even with identical premises. A candidate who reasons carefully but answers the wrong question type entirely will still mark the item wrong, especially under time pressure.

front: On the Logical Reasoning section, what exactly is the plausibility trap?
back: Choosing the answer that sounds like something that would realistically happen on the job instead of the answer the premises actually guarantee. Real-world plausibility and logical guarantee are not the same thing.

front: Officers on the downtown night beat report higher intoxication call rates than other beats. Constable Reyes has worked that beat six years. Is 'Reyes has handled more calls than any officer in the department' guaranteed?
back: No. The premise is a group rate comparing beats, not a personal total for Reyes. It says nothing about individual totals and does not rule out other officers who worked the same beat longer.

front: What mechanical check should you run whenever an answer option immediately feels right?
back: Ask which exact sentence, or combination of sentences, in the premises forces the option to be true. If you cannot point to specific wording that closes the gap, the option is not guaranteed, however sensible it sounds.

front: What mindset should you hold toward every answer option on this section?
back: Treat every conclusion as guilty until the premises prove it innocent. Do not credit an option for sounding reasonable; only credit it once you can point to the exact wording that guarantees it.

front: Rule: if a cruiser's dashcam fails, the officer files an equipment fault report. Officer Singh filed no equipment fault report today. What follows?
back: Singh's dashcam did not fail today. This is the valid contrapositive: no fault report guarantees no dashcam failure, since every dashcam failure triggers a report and none happened here.

front: Using the dashcam rule, is 'Singh's dashcam did not fail, so Singh filed no fault report' a valid conclusion?
back: No, this reverses the reasoning and denies the antecedent. It wrongly assumes dashcam failure is the only reason to file a fault report, when other equipment issues could also trigger one.

front: Using the dashcam rule, is 'Officer Singh filed a fault report, so the dashcam failed' a valid conclusion?
back: No, this affirms the consequent. The rule only guarantees a report when the dashcam fails; the report could have been filed for an entirely different piece of faulty equipment.

front: All K9 handlers complete advanced scent-detection training. Constable Nowak completed advanced scent-detection training. Is 'Nowak is a K9 handler' valid?
back: No, this is invalid, the undistributed middle again. Nowak only has to sit inside the training circle. Other roles, like evidence technicians, could also complete the same training without being K9 handlers.
